newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Battered traders still steer clear of Thai baht.
newsitem.headline: Battered traders still steer clear of Thai baht.

text.p: Trading volume in the baht has been minimal since the Thai government stunned markets on Wednesday by adopting a managed float system that effectively devalued the currency.

The move followed weeks of turmoil in Thailand's financial markets, with the baht under attack in May from overseas speculators concerned over the economy, a slump in the stock market and the shaky political backdrop.

Since then, coordinated central bank intervention, the imposition of capital controls and a sharp rise in interest rates left many speculators badly burned, and most want to keep a low profile until there is less volatility.
"I'm not interested at the moment. I'll want to let it all settle down before I go back in," the head of trading at a European bank said.

The baht has stabilised after plunging by nearly 20 percent in offshore markets on news of the managed float. On Friday, the Bank of Thailand allowed its new daily reference rate for the currency to weaken slightly to 28.189 to the dollar from 27.383 on Thursday.

In offshore markets, the baht was quoted at around 28.650/28.800 early on Friday. But the European trader noted that dealing spreads were still exceptionally wide with some banks quoting as much as a big figure (one baht) spread.
Wide spreads, where the bid and offer rate are far apart, are a sign a dealer does not want to be caught out on either side.
"That's a plain signal they're (dealers) not too interested either," he said. "But eventually things will slide back and the market will behave a little more normally. Then I'll have a look."

The baht's nemesis came on May 14 when it sank to 26.600 per U.S. dollar from an opening 25.920 as foreign speculators, including hedge funds, moved in for the kill as talk swirled of a possible baht devalution.

"At that stage the market was going crazy and the world and his wife seem to want to get involved and go short baht both spot and forward," said one Singapore based trader. "It was seen as a one-way-street."

But the authorities returned the market's volley with joint intervention by the Thai and Singapore central banks, and while volume in spot dried up, the forward market was still roaring ahead as a severe shortage of baht saw forward rates romp higher.

With the speculators already squeezed, the Bank of Thailand then introduced capital controls which prevented offshore players from raising baht in the spot market to either cover their short positions or take out fresh ones.
The two-tier market was then born as offshore traders were starved of liquidity and the dollar/baht rate strengthened dramatically as investors scrambled to cover their shorts.
From the 26.600 per dollar level the baht reached at the height of the attack, it subsequently rallied to 22.10 per dollar as demand for baht offshore far outpaced supply.

Hungarian financier George Soros, the man who made $1 billion during the 1992 sterling crisis, was rumoured to have taken a $4 billion short baht forward contract, although many traders doubt his position was, or is, that big. Soros himself said "there have been some exaggerated rumours".
By then, battered and bloody speculators had either lost a lot of money or were having sleepless nights over short positions they were hanging on to.
The dramatic announcement of the managed float on Wednesday this week allowed the baht to sink below the 28.00 per dollar level, which may seem like good news for the offshore punters.
But it came too late for many who had lost money by cutting and running after covering their short positions soon after the Bank of Thailand's successful defence of the baht.
Traders are still unsure of just how the new currency regime will work and as they lick their wounds, volume is likely to remain extremely light until further details are forthcoming.
"I'm fed up with the whole affair. There's very little liquidity and frankly I don't trust a thing that the (Thai) authorities say any more," a trader at a European bank said.

He added that the events of the last two days seemed to have mentally drained a lot of dealers. "Everyone's just looking forward to the weekend. It's a real Friday feeling today, especially with the States out for the Fourth of July."
"I'm taking a long lunch today."
